stumbles.quote: Round 1 measured only that configuration and concluded that domain vocabulary does not help much. Round 2 traced the small saving to the pre-tokenizer
stumbles.why: Rounds 1 and 2 are never introduced; the reader doesn't know these are earlier experiment stages or where they are documented. It also isn't clear whether the 21% and 8% figures come from Round 2.

stumbles.quote: Neither has tried a domain token table, and so no published clinical ModernBERT has either.
stumbles.why: This is a logical leap. Two models are named, but the claim covers all published clinical ModernBERTs, and the text gives no evidence for that.
Oskar is not introduced, so the reader doesn't know who he is or why his question matters. The quote also has an ellipsis in the middle.

stumbles.quote: A follow-up experiment, lifesci-ettin, trains models on the new table.
stumbles.why: The tense is unclear. It could mean the experiment is planned or already done, and the text doesn't say where it lives or what it found.

stumbles.quote: Yes. A life-sciences vocabulary makes Ettin cheaper on PubMed text
stumbles.why: The text never says what "cheaper" means. Only token count per abstract is given, and nothing about compute or cost. "Yes" also answers a question the text hasn't stated yet.

stumbles.quote: BioClinical ModernBERT and Clinical ModernBERT ship Ettin's tokenizer unchanged.
stumbles.why: Ettin and ModernBERT are never explained, and neither is how they relate. The reader can't tell why models named ModernBERT would use Ettin's tokenizer.

point: Retraining a 50K BPE vocabulary on PubMed abstracts cuts tokens per abstract by 21% versus Ettin's tokenizer, but only if the GPT-2 pre-tokenizer is also replaced with whitespace-only splitting. Retraining only the table saves 8%.
